q: What is a common sign of a phishing email?
options: It comes from a known contact
It contains urgent requests and suspicious links
explanation: Phishing messages usually pressure you to act fast and push you towards a link. A familiar logo proves nothing, because logos are easy to copy.

q: Which of the following passwords is most secure?
explanation: Length and variety make a password hard to guess. Short, common or predictable choices like “Password123” and “123456” are tried first by attackers.

q: What does HTTPS indicate?
explanation: HTTPS means the connection between you and the site is encrypted. It does not prove the site is honest, so still check the address.

q: What is ransomware?
options: Software that demands payment to unlock files
explanation: Ransomware locks or encrypts your files and demands payment. Offline backups are the best protection.

q: How should you connect to public Wi-Fi safely?
explanation: A VPN encrypts your traffic on a network you don’t control. Avoid logging in to sensitive accounts on public Wi-Fi where you can.

q: What makes a password strong?
options: A long phrase with numbers and symbols
explanation: A long passphrase is much harder to guess than a short word. Never use birthdays or the word “password”.

q: Which URL is most secure to enter your credentials?
explanation: Only enter credentials on addresses that start with https:// and belong to the real site. Plain http:// sends data unprotected.

q: What is a secure way to recover a forgotten password?
options: Using a link from a suspicious email
Using official site’s password reset form
explanation: Always use the official site or app’s reset form. Reset links in unexpected emails are a common phishing trick.

q: What is the main goal of a firewall?
options: Prevent unauthorized access to a network
explanation: A firewall filters traffic and blocks unauthorised connections to your network or device.

scenario: An email claims your account is locked and asks you to log in using a suspicious link.
q: What is the most likely threat?
explanation: An email that says your account is locked and pushes you to log in through a link is classic phishing. Open the official app or site yourself instead.

scenario: A login page looks like your bank’s, but the domain is "secure-login-info.net".
q: What kind of attack is shown?
explanation: A look-alike page on a different domain is a spoofed website. Always read the domain, not just the design.

scenario: A user connects to public Wi-Fi without encryption while checking their bank account.
q: What risk is involved here?
explanation: On an unencrypted network, other people can intercept what you send. That is eavesdropping.

scenario: A flashlight app requests access to your contacts, camera, and files.
q: What is suspicious about this app?
explanation: A flashlight app has no reason to read your contacts or files. Permissions should match what the app does.

scenario: A fake antivirus alert says “Your PC is infected! Click here to fix.”
q: What type of attack is likely happening?
explanation: Fake virus alerts that push you to click or call are a form of malicious advertising (malvertising) and often lead to malware or scams.

scenario: A QR code on a flyer redirects users to a fake login page.
q: What is this tactic called?
explanation: A QR code can hide a link to a fake login page. Scan only codes from sources you trust and check the address that opens.

scenario: A message appears: “Your files are encrypted. Pay Bitcoin to recover them.”
q: What kind of malware is this?
explanation: Files encrypted with a Bitcoin demand are ransomware. Don’t pay; disconnect the device and seek help.

scenario: A browser extension asks for full access to “all websites you visit.”
q: What is the concern with this request?
explanation: An extension that can read all your websites can see passwords and messages. Install only what you need, from trusted publishers.

scenario: A browser pop-up says “Verify your identity to continue” with a fake login form.
q: What’s happening here?
explanation: A pop-up asking you to “verify your identity” is trying to steal your login details: credential phishing.

scenario: A user enters a URL like "gooogle.com" and lands on a fake clone.
q: What technique is used here?
explanation: Typosquatting uses a misspelled web address (like “gooogle.com”) to trick people who mistype.

scenario: A popup says “Call this number immediately to fix your computer virus.”
q: What threat does this represent?
explanation: Genuine companies don’t show pop-ups telling you to phone a number. This is a fake tech support scam.

scenario: A user receives an SMS with a link claiming they’ve won a prize.
q: What attack method is this?
explanation: Phishing by SMS is called smishing. Prize messages with links are a favourite scam.

scenario: A fake login form records everything typed.
q: What is the threat technique used here?
explanation: A keylogger records what you type, including passwords. Fake forms and malware can both do this.

scenario: A user posts their birthday, full name, and high school online.
q: What risk does this behavior create?
explanation: Sharing your full name, birthday and school publicly gives scammers material for impersonation and social engineering.

scenario: A system sends a text code after password entry.
q: What security measure is shown here?
explanation: A code sent to your phone after your password is two-factor authentication (2FA). It stops attackers who only know your password.

scenario: A stranger hands out free USB drives at an event.
q: What should you suspect?
explanation: Unknown USB drives can carry malware. Never plug in a drive you were handed by a stranger.

scenario: A spreadsheet with thousands of emails and passwords is posted online.
q: What incident has occurred?
explanation: Leaked lists of emails and passwords are the result of a data breach. Change reused passwords and enable 2FA.

scenario: A targeted message uses your name and job title, asking you to confirm payroll info.
q: What phishing type is this?
explanation: A message that uses your name and job title to make a request is spear phishing: targeted, not mass-mailed.

scenario: A padlock icon is missing from a website’s address bar.
q: What does this likely indicate?
explanation: No padlock or HTTPS means the connection is not protected. Avoid entering any personal data.

scenario: A hidden service grants remote access to a system without user consent.
q: What is this vulnerability called?
explanation: A backdoor is a hidden way into a system that bypasses normal login controls.

scenario: A user receives a call claiming to be from their bank requesting their account number.
q: What kind of attack is this?
explanation: A caller claiming to be your bank and asking for details is vishing (voice phishing). Hang up and call the number on your card.

scenario: A browser extension injects ads into every site visited.
q: What kind of software is this?
explanation: Software that injects ads into every page is adware. Remove the extension and scan your device.

scenario: A game site uses a Facebook login button to collect data.
q: What risk might this pose?
explanation: Social login buttons on unfamiliar sites can share more of your data than you intend. Check what is requested.

scenario: A warning urges you to install a browser update from an unknown source.
q: What should you do?
explanation: Update software from the official source only. Pop-ups urging a browser update are a common malware trick.

scenario: An app requests camera access to offer voice features.
q: Why is this suspicious?
explanation: Camera access for a voice feature doesn’t match. When a permission doesn’t fit the app’s purpose, deny it.

scenario: Malware copies credentials from clipboard.
q: What threat type is this?
explanation: Clipper malware swaps the wallet or account number you copied with the attacker’s. Always re-check before sending money.

scenario: Someone offers to share their personal hotspot for free access.
q: What is the risk?
explanation: A free hotspot from a stranger lets them watch your traffic (network sniffing). Use trusted networks.

scenario: A URL is shown as “paypal.com” but actually links to “paypa1.com”.
q: What is this technique?
explanation: Swapping a letter for a lookalike (“paypa1”) is typosquatting. Read addresses carefully.

scenario: A webcam light turns on by itself unexpectedly.
q: What should you suspect?
explanation: A webcam light that turns on by itself can indicate a remote access tool. Disconnect, scan and change passwords.

scenario: A user uses the same password for email, banking, and work accounts.
q: What is the risk here?
explanation: Reusing one password everywhere lets attackers try a leaked password on all your accounts: credential stuffing.

scenario: A tool secretly records user activity and sends it to a remote server.
q: What is this software called?
explanation: Software that secretly records your activity and sends it away is spyware.

scenario: A website lacks HTTPS and shows a “Not Secure” warning.
q: What should you do?
explanation: If a site isn’t HTTPS and shows “Not secure”, don’t enter data on it.

scenario: Someone watches as you type your password on your phone in public.
q: What tactic is this?
explanation: Watching someone type their password or PIN is shoulder surfing. Shield the screen and keypad.

scenario: An email claims to be from your boss, but uses a public domain (e.g., Gmail).
q: What should raise suspicion?
explanation: A “boss” writing from a public email domain is a red flag. Confirm through a separate, known channel.

scenario: A fake invoice arrives with a new bank account for payment.
q: What attack does this represent?
explanation: A sudden change of bank details on an invoice is invoice fraud. Verify by phoning a known number before paying.

scenario: A password recovery form asks: “What’s your pet’s name?”
q: What makes this insecure?
explanation: Answers like a pet’s name can be found on social media. Use unique answers or skip such questions.

scenario: A router uses “admin/admin” as its login credentials.
q: What’s the risk?
explanation: Default logins such as admin/admin are widely known. Change router passwords at setup.

scenario: A user activates a VPN before joining hotel Wi-Fi.
q: Why is this good practice?
explanation: A VPN encrypts your traffic, which helps on untrusted networks like hotels and cafés.

scenario: A notification asks you to install security updates.
q: What’s the best action?
explanation: Install updates only from your device’s official update system or app store.

scenario: An email from “admin@secure-pay.com” asks for your payment information.
q: What’s the most likely threat?
explanation: A payment request from an unfamiliar look-alike address is most likely phishing. Verify through official channels.

scenario: A fake message appears to come from your CEO asking for an urgent wire transfer.
q: What type of attack is this?
explanation: Impersonating a senior executive to request urgent action is whaling, a form of targeted phishing.

scenario: A popup pretends to be a browser update but installs malware instead.
q: What best describes this?
explanation: A fake “update” pop-up that installs malware is a common trick. Update only through official channels.

scenario: A public Wi-Fi warning pops up with "Unsecured network."
q: Safest response?
explanation: On a network flagged as unsecured, use a VPN or avoid sensitive tasks.

scenario: A password input with the example '123456'.
q: How strong is the password?
explanation: “123456” is among the most common passwords and is guessed within seconds.

scenario: A message asks you to send a code urgently to help a "friend" locked out of their account.
q: What tactic is used?
explanation: Urgent requests to send a code “for a friend” are social engineering. Call the friend to confirm; never share one-time codes.

scenario: A mobile app on the store has poor reviews, suspicious grammar, and excessive permissions.
q: What is the biggest red flag?
explanation: Poor reviews and bad grammar suggest a fake app. Check the publisher and install only from official stores.

scenario: A website looks identical to your bank’s homepage but the URL says "mybanc-login.com".
q: What is this an example of?
explanation: A page that looks identical but sits on a different address is a spoofed website.

scenario: A user visits a sketchy website and malware installs automatically without clicking anything.
q: What kind of attack is this?
explanation: Malware that installs just from visiting a site is a drive-by download. Keep browsers updated.

scenario: A poster on a public wall displays a QR code claiming to offer free Wi-Fi.
q: What cyber threat could this represent?
explanation: A QR code on a wall can lead to a fake page: phishing via QR code. Check where it goes before you log in.

scenario: A computer suddenly slows down, shows pop-ups, and antivirus is disabled.
q: What is the most likely cause?
explanation: Sudden slowness, pop-ups and disabled antivirus strongly suggest a malware infection.

q: What is cybersecurity?
options: Protecting devices, accounts and data from digital threats
explanation: Cybersecurity is the practice of protecting people, devices, networks and data from digital attacks and misuse.

q: Who can be a target of cybercrime?
options: Anyone who uses a phone, email or the internet
explanation: Criminals target everyone, because ordinary people often have fewer protections than organisations.

q: Which habit protects you against the widest range of attacks?
options: Keeping software updated and using unique passwords with 2FA
Using the same password everywhere so you remember it
explanation: Updates, unique passwords and two-factor authentication close the most common doors attackers use.

q: What does the “CIA triad” in security stand for?
explanation: It describes three goals: keep data private, keep it accurate and unaltered, and keep it available when needed.

q: You see an alarming message about your account. What is the best first step?
options: Click the link quickly before it’s too late
Pause, then check through the official app or website you open yourself
Forward it to everyone in your contacts
explanation: Attackers rely on rushing you. Slow down and verify through a channel you trust.

q: Which is the strongest choice for an important account?
options: A long passphrase of several unrelated words plus a number
explanation: Length matters most. A passphrase of unrelated words is both strong and memorable.

q: What does a password manager do?
options: Stores unique strong passwords for you behind one master password
explanation: A manager lets you use a different strong password everywhere without memorising them all.

q: Why is reusing one password on many accounts risky?
options: If one site is breached, attackers can try it on your other accounts
explanation: Leaked passwords are tried on other sites automatically. Unique passwords limit the damage.

q: Which second factor is generally safest?
options: An authenticator app or a hardware security key
A code you read out to anyone who asks
explanation: Authenticator apps and security keys are harder to intercept than SMS codes. Never share a code with anyone.

q: Someone claiming to be support asks for the one-time code just sent to you. What should you do?
options: Give it to them to prove it’s you
Refuse. Real support never needs your one-time code
explanation: A one-time code is a key to your account. Anyone asking for it is trying to take it over.

scenario: A text message creates urgency and asks for your BVN and OTP.
q: A text says: “Your account will be blocked in 30 minutes. Confirm your BVN and OTP at bit.ly/xyz.” What is the best response?
options: Tap the link and confirm quickly
Ignore the link and contact your bank using its official app or number
explanation: Banks don’t ask for OTPs or full details by SMS link. Contact the bank through official channels.

q: Which detail is the strongest sign of a phishing email?
options: The sender address doesn’t match the company’s real domain
explanation: Check the actual sender address. Look-alike domains are a common trick.

q: You hover over a link and the address shown is different from the text. What does that suggest?
options: The link may lead somewhere other than it claims
The message is from a friend
explanation: Mismatched link text and destination is a classic phishing sign.

q: You clicked a suspicious link and typed your password. What should you do first?
options: Change that password at once on the real site, enable 2FA and check your account activity
explanation: Act quickly: change the password (and anywhere you reused it), enable 2FA and review recent activity.

q: What is social engineering?
options: Manipulating people into giving up information or access
A way of building social media apps
explanation: Social engineering targets people rather than technology, using trust, urgency or fear.

q: A caller says they are from your telecom company and need your PIN “to fix a problem”. What should you do?
options: Hang up and call the official number yourself
Ask them to send you a link
explanation: Never share PINs or codes on an incoming call. Call back using a number you find yourself.

q: Which of these is a typical pressure tactic?
options: “You have plenty of time to think about it.”
“You can check with your bank first.”
explanation: Urgency stops you from thinking. Slowing down is the best defence.

q: A stranger at the office door says they forgot their badge and asks to follow you inside. What is the safest action?
options: Let them in to be polite
Politely direct them to reception to be verified
explanation: Following someone through a secured door (tailgating) is a common physical attack. Use the proper process.

q: An “investment” promises 50% returns every week with no risk. What is the likely situation?
options: A scam. Guaranteed high returns with no risk are a major warning sign
explanation: Real investments carry risk. Promises of fast, guaranteed profit are typical of Ponzi and fake-investment schemes.

q: You receive a message that you won a lottery you never entered. They ask for a “release fee”. What is this?
explanation: If you must pay to receive a prize, it’s a scam.

q: A new loan app asks for access to your contacts and photos before lending. What is the safest approach?
options: Allow everything to get the loan
Avoid it. Use only licensed lenders and never give broad access to your data
explanation: Some predatory loan apps misuse contacts and photos to harass borrowers. Use regulated lenders only.

q: A buyer overpays you by cheque or transfer and asks you to refund the difference. What is going on?
options: A likely overpayment scam. The original payment may be fake or reversed
explanation: The scammer’s payment later fails, but your refund is real money gone.

q: Someone you met online asks for money for an emergency but can’t video call. What does this suggest?
options: A possible romance or impersonation scam
explanation: Avoid sending money to people you haven’t met in person, however convincing the story.

q: Before buying from an unknown online shop, which check is most useful?
options: Whether the page has nice photos
Searching for independent reviews and using pay-on-delivery or a protected payment method
Whether the price is very low
explanation: Fake shops copy nice designs. Independent reviews and protected payments reduce your risk.

q: A job advert asks you to pay a fee to secure the position. What is the best action?
options: Walk away. Genuine employers don’t charge applicants to hire them
Ask a friend to pay too
explanation: Fee-for-a-job requests are a common recruitment scam.

q: Which setting best protects your phone if it is lost or stolen?
options: A strong screen lock plus find-my-device
No lock so you can open it fast
explanation: A lock stops casual access, and find-my-device lets you locate, lock or erase the phone.

q: Where should you install apps from?
options: Random websites offering free paid apps
explanation: Official stores check apps. APK files from unknown sources often carry malware.

q: Why install phone updates promptly?
options: They fix security flaws attackers use
explanation: Updates patch known vulnerabilities.

q: What is SIM swap fraud?
options: A criminal moves your number to their SIM to receive your calls and codes
explanation: Once they control your number they can intercept OTPs. Contact your network provider immediately if your SIM suddenly stops working.

q: Your phone suddenly loses all network signal and you didn’t do anything. What could be a warning sign?
options: Possibly a SIM swap. Contact your network provider and bank immediately
explanation: Unexpected loss of service can mean your number was moved. Act fast.

q: What should you check before typing a password on a website?
options: That the address is the real site and starts with https://
That the page has a colourful design
That someone shared it on social media
explanation: Read the address carefully. Look-alike domains are common.

q: A website offers a free download of paid software. What is the safest choice?
options: Avoid it. Cracked software often contains malware
explanation: Pirated software is a common way to spread malware.

q: What does incognito or private browsing do?
options: Hides you from your internet provider and websites
Stops your browser saving history on that device only
explanation: It doesn’t make you anonymous online. It only avoids saving history locally.

q: Which information is risky to post publicly?
options: A photo of your boarding pass or ID
explanation: Boarding passes, IDs and tickets contain details criminals can reuse.

q: A friend’s account sends you a strange link and asks for money. What should you do?
options: Contact your friend on another channel. The account may be hacked
explanation: Hijacked accounts are used to scam contacts.

q: Which privacy setting is wise for most personal accounts?
options: Limit who can see your posts, contacts and phone number
Make everything public for more followers
Use the same password as email
explanation: Review settings regularly. The less public detail, the less scammers can use.

q: WhatsApp sends you a 6-digit verification code you didn’t request. What does this mean?
options: Someone may be trying to register your number. Do not share the code
You must reply with the code
explanation: Sharing it lets the attacker take over your WhatsApp. Enable two-step verification.

q: What is a safe way to deal with a friend request from a stranger?
options: Check mutual contacts and the profile, and decline if unsure
explanation: Fake profiles are used for scams and impersonation.

q: Which is personal data you should protect?
options: Your BVN, NIN and date of birth
explanation: Government IDs and financial identifiers should be shared only when truly necessary and with legitimate organisations.

q: Before an app collects your information, what should you ask?
options: Does it really need this data and how will it be used?
How many downloads does it have?
explanation: Share the minimum data needed.

q: What does end-to-end encryption in a messaging app mean?
options: Only you and the recipient can read the messages
The company can read all messages
explanation: Only the people in the conversation have the keys to read the content.

q: Which statement about data protection law in Nigeria is most accurate?
options: Individuals have rights over how their personal data is handled under the Nigeria Data Protection Act
Companies can use your data however they like
explanation: The Nigeria Data Protection Act 2023 sets duties for organisations and rights for individuals. Read official guidance for details.

q: You’re asked for your NIN to enter a competition. What is the best approach?
options: Ask why it’s needed and refuse if the reason isn’t clear and legitimate
explanation: Share identity numbers only with organisations that have a genuine reason.

q: Which action best protects against ransomware?
options: Keeping offline or cloud backups you can restore from
explanation: With a good backup you can restore without paying.

q: Which is a typical way malware spreads?
options: Unexpected email attachments and fake downloads
explanation: Don’t open unexpected attachments, and download only from trusted sources.

q: Your device seems infected. What is a sensible first step?
options: Disconnect from the internet and run a trusted security scan
explanation: Cutting the connection limits spread and data loss.

q: What is the first thing to change on a new home router?
explanation: Default passwords are widely known. Use a long unique one.

q: What does a firewall do?
options: Filters network traffic according to security rules
explanation: A firewall blocks unwanted connections.

q: Why should you update router firmware?
explanation: Manufacturers release updates to patch security holes.

q: Which Wi-Fi security setting is best for your home network today?
options: WPA3, or WPA2 if WPA3 isn’t available
explanation: Use the strongest supported protocol and a long passphrase.

q: You see two networks named “Airport_Free_WiFi” and “AirportWiFi”. What should you do?
options: Ask staff for the official network name
explanation: Attackers create look-alike hotspots (evil twins).

q: Which is an early warning sign of identity theft?
options: Transactions or accounts you don’t recognise
explanation: Review statements and alerts regularly.

q: How should you dispose of papers containing personal details?
options: Leave them in the bin whole
explanation: Criminals can reuse documents like bank statements and ID copies.

q: Someone uses your details to open an account. What should you do?
options: Report it to the institution and relevant authorities and secure your accounts
explanation: Speed limits damage. Keep records of what you report.

q: When sharing a photocopy of your ID card, what is a good habit?
options: Write the purpose and date across it
Give it to anyone who asks
explanation: Marking a copy with its purpose makes misuse harder.

q: You get a message offering a scholarship if you pay a processing fee. What is the likely situation?
explanation: Legitimate scholarships don’t ask applicants for money to be selected.

q: Why shouldn’t you share your student portal password with friends?
options: They could change your records or misuse your account
It’s fine if they are trusted
explanation: Shared credentials can lead to account misuse you are responsible for.

q: Which is safest on shared university computers?
options: Log out completely and don’t save passwords in the browser
explanation: Always sign out and clear saved sessions.

q: Free study app asks for access to your contacts and microphone. What do you do?
explanation: Apps should only request what they need.

q: What is a simple first step for an SME to reduce cyber risk?
options: Use unique passwords, 2FA and regular backups
explanation: Basic hygiene prevents most common attacks.

q: Your accountant emails new bank details for a supplier payment. What should you do?
options: Confirm by phoning a known number before paying
explanation: Business email compromise relies on fake changes of payment details.

q: Why should staff have only the access they need?
options: Limiting access reduces damage if an account is compromised
It is a legal requirement everywhere
explanation: This is the principle of least privilege.

q: Where should business backups be kept?
options: Somewhere separate from the main system, and tested
explanation: A backup that is attached to the infected system can be lost too.

q: A former employee still has access to company accounts. What should you do?
explanation: Offboarding should include revoking all access.

q: What is the purpose of cybersecurity awareness training in an organisation?
options: To help staff recognise and report threats
explanation: People are a key line of defence. Training works best alongside technical controls.

q: What is a good culture around reporting suspicious emails?
explanation: Quick reporting helps stop incidents early.

q: What is an incident response plan?
options: A prepared set of steps and contacts for handling a security incident
explanation: Preparing before an incident saves time when it matters.

q: Which policy helps protect staff using personal phones for work?
options: Screen locks, updates and the ability to remotely wipe work data
explanation: Basic mobile device rules reduce risk.

q: Who may legitimately ask for your card PIN or OTP?
explanation: Your PIN and OTP are for you alone.

q: What is a safe habit at an ATM or POS?
options: Shield the keypad and don’t accept help from strangers
Share your PIN to speed things up
explanation: Watch for shoulder surfing and tampered machines.

q: You get a debit alert for a transaction you didn’t make. What should you do first?
options: Contact your bank immediately through official channels and block the card
explanation: Speed matters. Use the bank’s official app or number.

q: A seller asks you to pay by gift cards or to a personal account for a “deposit”. What is the safest approach?
options: Don’t pay. Use protected payment methods
explanation: Untraceable payments are favoured by scammers.

q: Before you confirm a transfer, what should you double-check?
options: The account name and number shown
explanation: Confirm the beneficiary name before sending.

q: What is a good habit for online shopping?
options: Use a virtual or low-balance card and check statements
Save your card on every site
explanation: Limiting exposure reduces the loss if details leak.

q: Which statement about AI chatbots is the safest to follow?
options: Don’t paste passwords, ID numbers or confidential data into them
explanation: Treat chat inputs as potentially stored or reviewed.

q: What is a deepfake?
options: Synthetic audio, image or video that imitates a real person
explanation: Deepfakes can be used to impersonate people in scams.

q: You receive a voice note that sounds like a relative asking for urgent money. What should you do?
options: Verify by calling them back on a known number
explanation: Voice cloning exists. Always verify through a second channel.

q: How can attackers use AI?
options: To write convincing phishing messages at scale
explanation: AI can polish scam messages, so don’t rely on spotting spelling errors alone.

q: Which is a good practice when using AI answers?
options: Verify important facts from trusted sources
Trust them for medical or legal decisions
explanation: AI can be wrong while sounding confident.
